articles.title: Why the Rams make sense for J.J. McCarthy after losing the Vikings’ starting job
articles.standfirst: One destination stands above the rest for the former national champion with Michigan
articles.summary: One destination stands above the rest for the former national champion with Michigan
articles.body:
T he Minnesota Vikings entered training camp expecting a competitive quarterback battle. Two weeks later, the contest was over.

Head coach Kevin O’Connell named Kyler Murray the team's starting quarterback, ending any realistic chance of J.J. McCarthy opening the season atop the depth chart.

For the former No. 10 overall pick, the decision represents another setback in what has been an unexpectedly difficult start to his NFL career. Now the question becomes whether McCarthy's future remains in Minnesota at all.

NFL.com senior news writer Kevin Patra recently suggested that the Vikings should consider moving on from the third-year quarterback if a trade opportunity emerges. While Patra does not expect Minnesota to release McCarthy , he argued that the organization would likely trust veteran Carson Wentz more than McCarthy as the primary backup should Murray miss time.

In that scenario, McCarthy could find himself buried as the team's third quarterback despite entering the league with first-round expectations.

If the Vikings ultimately decide to explore trade options, several teams could show interest. However, one destination stands above the rest: the Los Angeles Rams.

Why Minnesota could consider a trade

Quarterback depth is valuable in today's NFL , but so is roster flexibility.

The Vikings acquired Murray with the expectation that he would lead a roster capable of competing for a playoff spot. Wentz provides a veteran insurance policy with extensive starting experience, and Minnesota's coaching staff appears comfortable with his ability to step into the lineup if necessary.

That leaves McCarthy in an awkward position. Quarterbacks selected in the first round rarely thrive when stuck in developmental limbo for multiple seasons. At some point, teams need answers. Is the player a future starter, a reliable backup, or simply a draft investment that did not work out?

If Minnesota no longer views McCarthy as a legitimate challenger to Murray , moving him while he still possesses upside could be the most logical outcome.

Why the Rams are the ideal landing spot

The Rams have mastered the art of quarterback development under head coach Sean McVay . While Matthew Stafford continues to play at a high level, he is nearing the final stages of an accomplished career. Los Angeles has consistently searched for long-term answers behind its veteran starter, understanding that succession planning is essential in a league driven by quarterback play.

McCarthy would arrive without the pressure of immediately saving a franchise. Instead, he could spend a season learning McVay's system while refining the traits that made him a first-round selection.

His strengths align well with what the Rams value offensively. McCarthy has shown mobility, accuracy on the move, and the ability to operate within a structured passing game. Those qualities could flourish in an offense built around play-action concepts, timing routes, and quarterback-friendly designs.

Just as important, Los Angeles offers stability. Young quarterbacks often struggle because they land in chaotic situations with frequent coaching changes and weak supporting casts. The Rams provide the opposite environment: an established offensive coach, proven infrastructure, and a front office with a track record of maximizing talent.

For a former top-10 pick, sitting as a third quarterback is rarely a long-term solution. That is why a trade may ultimately benefit everyone involved. Minnesota could gain draft capital, McCarthy could receive a fresh start, and a quarterback-needy franchise could acquire a talented player who still has plenty of untapped potential. If that scenario unfolds, the Rams appear to be the team best positioned to unlock it.

articles.title: Should Vikings fans be worried? Kyler Murray’s latest injury reignites durability questions
articles.standfirst: The quarterback exited the game in the first quarter after suffering a concussion and did not return
articles.summary: The quarterback exited the game in the first quarter after suffering a concussion and did not return
articles.body:
T he Minnesota Vikings could not have asked for a much better result in their Week 1 showdown against the Green Bay Packers. They rallied for a convincing 39-22 victory at U.S. Bank Stadium and began the season with a statement win over a division rival.

The celebration, however, came with a significant concern. Starting quarterback Kyler Murray exited the game in the first quarter after suffering a concussion and did not return. On a third-and-seven scramble, Murray slid before taking a hard hit from Packers defenders Lukas Van Ness and Javon Bullard. His helmet came off on the play, and he remained on the turf before eventually walking off under his own power.

Head coach Kevin O'Connell offered little clarity after the game. “I have no update on how those evaluations have gone,” O'Connell said. “We'll take it day by day and see how he comes in tomorrow.” The injury immediately reignited a familiar conversation that has followed Murray throughout much of his NFL career: Can he stay healthy?

Does Murray deserves the injury-prone label?

At first glance, the answer appears troubling. Murray has missed 30 games during his seven NFL seasons entering the 2026 campaign, a figure that represents 25.6 percent of the 117 regular-season games his teams have played during that span. Any franchise investing in a quarterback wants better availability than that.

But the deeper context tells a more nuanced story. The perception around Murray i s that he has been constantly sidelined by a long list of injuries. In reality, much of the missed time stems from two major setbacks rather than a continuous stream of recurring ailments.

Of the 30 games Murray has missed, 27 came because of just two injuries. The biggest was the torn ACL he suffered late in the 2022 season, an injury that also impacted much of his 2023 campaign as he worked his way back to full health. Technically, Murray did not miss those games because of a new injury in 2023; he was still recovering from one of the most serious injuries an NFL player can suffer.

Another significant chunk of missed time came during the 2025 season. While the foot injury that sidelined him was legitimate, there is reason to believe he may have been able to return before the season ended. The Arizona Cardinals ultimately chose a cautious approach, shutting him down when his recovery failed to progress at the pace the organization had hoped. That distinction matters when evaluating whether Murray deserves the injury-prone label.

The Vikings should dismiss the concern entirely

Players who repeatedly suffer soft-tissue injuries, recurring muscle strains, or chronic issues that cause them to miss games year after year often earn that reputation. Murray's injury history looks different. Three times during his NFL career he played every game on the schedule. His missed time has largely been concentrated around a pair of significant injuries rather than a constant cycle of setbacks.

That doesn't mean the Vikings should dismiss the concern entirely. Quarterbacks who rely heavily on mobility inevitably expose themselves to more hits than traditional pocket passers. Murray's athleticism has always been one of his greatest strengths, but it also creates additional opportunities for defenders to make contact. Sunday's concussion was a reminder that even a routine scramble can turn dangerous in an instant.

The Vikings also have fresh memories of how quickly quarterback plans can unravel. Minnesota brought Murray in hoping he could provide stability and playmaking ability to an offense built around elite skill-position talent. Losing him for any extended period would significantly alter those plans, even with veteran backup Carson Wentz stepping in effectively against Green Bay.

Wentz completed 12 of 19 passes for 133 yards and three touchdowns after replacing Murray, helping Minnesota turn an early deficit into a comfortable victory. Still, the Vikings did not acquire Murray to watch from the sideline.

articles.title: Odell Beckham Jr. finds a new home with one of the NFL’s last undefeated teams
articles.standfirst: Beckham had no catches and was only on the field for 19 snaps across three games before the Giants cut him
articles.summary: Beckham had no catches and was only on the field for 19 snaps across three games before the Giants cut him
articles.body:
So far this season, the most surprising team has not been the 0-4 Houston Texans or Los Angeles Chargers , nor even the undefeated Kansas City Chiefs or San Francisco 49ers , but rather the Minnesota Vikings .

Sitting at a pristine 4-0 record , Minnesota has managed to win games despite stretches where their offense struggled to find the end zone, heavily relying on kicker Will Reichard and a ferocious, top-tier defense to carry them. However, if the Vikings want to make a deep playoff push , their offensive unit desperately needs an upgrade.

To address that need, the front office moved swiftly to incorporate veteran free-agent wide receiver Odell Beckham Jr. onto their practice squad, and head coach Kevin O'Connell has not ruled out the possibility of elevating him to the active roster in time for Sunday's matchup against the New Orleans Saints .

The 33-year-old wideout was cut loose by the New York Giants after recording zero catches and playing just 19 offensive snaps across three games.

Odell Beckham Jr. Reunites with Kevin O'Connell in the Vikings

Beckham’s arrival in Minnesota sparks a reunion with Kevin O'Connell , who served as the offensive coordinator for the Los Angeles Rams back in 2021 , the memorable midseason year when Beckham was traded from Cleveland to LA and ultimately hauled in a touchdown in the Super Bowl before suffering a knee injury that wiped out his entire 2022 campaign.

Now, with the Vikings' top two wideouts, Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison , dealing with injuries, and third-string option Jauan Jennings hauling in just two catches on four targets during his debut season with the franchise, Beckham provides immediate veteran depth.

He slots in alongside young second-year receivers Tai Felton and Myles Price, who have been alternating in the No. 4 and No. 5 roles.

O'Connell noted that the beauty of their playbook lies in foundational concepts and quick-learning mechanisms that allow new arrivals to pick up assignments rapidly if they are called up on game day.

Given that Beckham has not started more than 10 games in a single season since 2021 , this chapter in Minnesota could serve as a defining late-career stop as he attempts to inject life into the Vikings' offense through the remainder of the year.

articles.title: Odell Beckham Jr. steals JJ McCarthy's old Vikings number, and Justin Jefferson is the reason why
articles.standfirst: OBJ signed with the Minnesota Vikings on Wednesday and quickly picked out his new number.
articles.summary: OBJ signed with the Minnesota Vikings on Wednesday and quickly picked out his new number.
articles.body:
It didn't take very long for Odell Beckham Jr. to find a new home. His fairytale return to the New York Giants didn't go as planned, leading to his release from the franchise after Week 3. On Wednesday, OBJ was on a new team: the Minnesota Vikings .

Beckham was brought in as an insurance plan for Justin Jefferson , one of the league's top receivers who missed last game with an ankle injury. OBJ has a link to Jefferson due to both of them attending LSU , and he's also spent time with head coach Kevin O'Connell , when they were together on the Los Angeles Rams in 2021.

Beckham wasted no time picking out a new number, and his choice definitely raised some eyebrows. It's not uncommon for wide receiver to choose a single-digit number, but Beckham went with No. 9 . That, of course, was the jersey number of underwhelming first round pick J.J. McCarthy , who ironically is now with the Giants.

Odell Beckham Jr. says Justin Jefferson "got half his game from me"

When asked why he chose that number, it turns out it had nothing to do with McCarthy. Instead, OBJ went the humorous route and joked that he picked it because Jefferson "got half his game from me" .

Jefferson wears No. 18 , and he grew up watching Beckham in college with the Tigers. There are certainly some similarities with Beckham and Jefferson. In fact, Jefferson's historic start to his NFL career was only preceded by OBJ's incredible beginnings in the league . Now, it's all come full circle.

articles.title: Why it’s hard to bet against the Minnesota Vikings in 2026
articles.standfirst: The team doesn't necessarily need its offense to dominate every game if its defense can consistently disrupt opponents
articles.summary: The team doesn't necessarily need its offense to dominate every game if its defense can consistently disrupt opponents
articles.body:
The Minnesota Vikings are making a convincing case that a dominant defense can carry a team a long way in the NFL. And according to NFL.com analyst Bucky Brooks , that might be enough to make them one of the most dangerous contenders in the NFC. Minnesota is off to a 5-0 start, and its defense has been central to the team's success. After the Vikings defeated the New Orleans Saints 23-13, Brooks made the case that Brian Flores' aggressive defensive scheme could become a decisive advantage as the season progresses.

“If defense wins championships in 2026, it's hard to bet against these Vikings, ” Brooks wrote, pointing to Flores' relentless use of Cover 0 pressures and complementary blitzes to overwhelm opposing quarterbacks and play-callers.

The argument is straightforward: Minnesota doesn't necessarily need its offense to dominate every game if its defense can consistently disrupt opponents, create turnovers and give the offense favorable field position.

Brian Flores is making life miserable for opposing quarterbacks

Flores' defense is built around pressure, deception and forcing quarterbacks to make difficult decisions before they have time to settle into a rhythm. His aggressive approach frequently presents offenses with the threat of an all-out blitz.

Yet the Vikings don't always send every defender who appears poised to rush the passer. By disguising their intentions and changing coverages after the snap, they can leave quarterbacks uncertain about where the pressure is coming from and which receivers will be available.

That uncertainty is a significant part of the scheme's appeal. Offensive lines must identify potential rushers, running backs may be forced to stay in protection, and quarterbacks must process the defense quickly enough to avoid a costly mistake. When the protection breaks down, the results can be devastating: sacks, tackles for loss, hurried throws and turnovers.

Minnesota's early-season performance illustrates the impact. The Vikings recorded at least four sacks and forced at least two takeaways in each of their first three games, according to the team's official website. They also finished their Week 5 victory over New Orleans with two interceptions while limiting the Saints to 142 total yards.

Brooks believes that relentless pressure makes Minnesota especially difficult to face over four quarters. Opponents may find ways to counter individual blitzes, but sustaining that response for an entire game is another challenge.

Winning ugly could be Minnesota's biggest advantage

The Vikings' success isn't solely about how many points their offense scores. It's about how the defense changes the conditions under which the offense operates. A sack that forces a punt, an interception that ends a promising drive or a pressure that creates a short field can make the difference between an ordinary offensive possession and a scoring opportunity.

That's the kind of complementary football Brooks sees developing in Minnesota under head coach Kevin O'Connell. Quarterback Kyler Murray is settling into O'Connell's offensive system, and the Vikings have the potential to benefit from a quarterback who can threaten defenses with both his arm and his mobility. But Brooks' argument doesn't require Murray to carry the team by himself. Instead, Minnesota can lean on its defense while the offense focuses on protecting the football, sustaining drives and capitalizing on opportunities.

That approach also offers a practical path through games when the passing attack struggles or the offense fails to generate explosive plays consistently. The Vikings' 23-13 win over the Saints provided a recent example. Murray completed 24 of 30 passes for 229 yards and a touchdown, while running back Aaron Jones rushed for 113 yards and a score. Minnesota's defense , meanwhile, intercepted Shough twice and kept New Orleans from generating much offensive production.

The road to the NFC's top seed remains demanding

Brooks also identified the possibility of Minnesota making a run at the NFC's No. 1 seed. Finishing atop the conference would be a significant achievement, potentially providing home-field advantage throughout the NFC playoffs and a first-round bye.

The Vikings' unbeaten start gives them a strong foundation, but it does not guarantee that they will maintain their pace. The NFL season is long, and opponents will have opportunities to study Flores' pressure packages, develop protection adjustments and test Minnesota in different situations.

The defense also faces the inherent risk of an aggressive scheme: when a blitz fails to reach the quarterback, the secondary can be left exposed. If opponents consistently beat the pressure with quick throws or exploit isolated matchups , Minnesota may have to adjust its approach.

The offense's consistency will matter, too. A defense can create opportunities, but the Vikings still need to turn those chances into points and close out games. Murray's command of the system and O'Connell's ability to balance the passing and running games will be important as the competition intensifies.
